title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive exploration of both step choices versus a bottom-up 1D DP array.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array cost where cost[i] is the cost of stepping on stair i, and you may start from step 0 or step 1, and from any step can climb 1 or 2 steps, find the minimum cost to reach the top (just past the last stair).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","cost array"],["Output","Minimum total cost to reach past the final step"],["Goal","dp[i] = minimum cost to REACH step i, built from dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 steps"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Reach a position by taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, minimizing cost\"","A classic 1D DP: the cost to reach step i depends only on the cost to reach the two immediately preceding steps"]]}

blocks.text: Let dp[i] be the minimum cost to REACH step i (before paying to step further). Since a step can only be entered from one step back or two steps back, dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]); the answer is dp[n] (reaching past the last stair, index n, where n is the array length).

blocks.title: Analogy: Cheapest Way to Reach the Top of a Toll Staircase
blocks.text: Picture a staircase where every step charges a toll to step ON it, and you can hop up either 1 or 2 steps at a time. The cheapest way to reach any given step is whichever of the two immediately preceding steps, plus its toll, is cheaper.
Minimum cost = 15 (start at step 1, paying 15, then step directly to the top).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: dp[0] and dp[1] are both 0, since starting at either step 0 or step 1 costs nothing to REACH (the cost is paid only when leaving that step).

Observation 2: For i from 2 to n, dp[i] can only be reached from i-1 or i-2, paying that step's cost to leave it, so dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]).

Observation 3: The final answer is dp[n] (n being the array length), representing reaching just past the last stair.
This leads to a simple 1D bottom-up DP array, filled left to right using only the two previous values.
Recursively try both choices (stepping 1 or 2) from every position, without memoization, exploring every possible path to the top.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying both choices recursively directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same positions repeatedly across different paths, costing exponential time; a bottom-up DP array reuses previously computed results directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to n) without memoization.
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a bottom-up DP array computes each position's cost exactly once, reusing the two previous values directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a dp array of size n+1, with dp[0] = dp[1] = 0. For i from 2 to n, set dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]). Return dp[n].
Use a bottom-up 1D DP array, each entry computed once from the two previous entries.

Since any step can only be reached from exactly one step back or two steps back, dp[i] correctly captures the minimum cost to reach step i by considering both possible predecessors and their costs to leave; building this bottom-up ensures dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] are already correctly computed by the time dp[i] needs them.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the dp array (reducible to O(1) using two rolling variables).

blocks.text: Min Cost Climbing Stairs is a foundational 1D DP problem, directly analogous to the classic climbing stairs / Fibonacci-style recurrence.

items: Confusing "cost to reach step i" with "cost of step i itself", leading to an off-by-one error in the recurrence.
Forgetting the answer is dp[n] (past the last stair), not dp[n-1].

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Only 2 steps","The answer is simply the cheaper of the two starting steps."],["All costs are 0","The answer is 0."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "dp[i] is the cost to REACH step i, not step i's own cost" clarifies the recurrence precisely.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum cost to climb stairs, 1 or 2 at a time", think: a 1D DP array built from the two previous positions.

items: How would you reduce the space to O(1) using just two rolling variables instead of a full array?
Climbing Stairs and House Robber, both share this same "combine the two previous positions" 1D DP structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^n); the bottom-up DP array costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: 1D bottom-up dynamic programming, combining the two previous positions.
Core Idea: dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]), the cheapest way to REACH step i.
Time: O(2^n) for the brute force, O(n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(n) (reducible to O(1)) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: dp[i] tracks the cost to REACH a step, not the step's own cost.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy 1D DP problem.
One line memory trick: cheapest of the two steps behind, plus their cost.
